O12 already contains line 1: two P7 mugs at €18 each. Products P7 and P8 exist; P99 does not. Each proposal below starts from that same state.

What the experiment represents

With the intended rules, another P7 line and a P8 line pass. Repeating line 1, omitting quantity, setting it to zero, or naming P99 fail. The extra product-uniqueness rule would also reject the legitimate second P7 line.

EXPERIMENT · SAME ANSWER, DIFFERENT WORK
Finding the names on a receipt

Each purchase line needs one product name. Add lines to the receipt or unrelated products to the catalogue, then compare two ways of finding the matches.

RESULT · INPUTS AND ROUTE

2 products: P7 is Blue mug, P8 is Bowl. The receipt has 2 lines, alternating P7 and P8.

Take line 1 (P7). Compare its ID with all 2 products → Blue mug.
Take line 2 (P8). Compare its ID with all 2 products → Bowl.

4 product-ID comparisons; 2 result rows.

Receipt result · ordered by line number; amounts in EUR
Line	Product	Name	Amount
1	P7	Blue mug	20.00
2	P8	Bowl	24.00

Building the lookup would instead store 2 product entries and make 2 probes. Both methods return the same 2 rows.

Try 200 products and 6 lines. Switch methods without changing the data. Then reduce the receipt to 1 line: how much of the lookup-building work remains?

This browser model counts full-scan comparisons, lookup entries and probes separately; they are not equal units of time. It omits indexes, early stopping, hash collisions, memory limits, disk access and sorting costs. The added receipt lines and products belong only to this experiment. No PostgreSQL query runs here.

The two-line example above is complete. Enable JavaScript to vary it. With 200 products and 6 lines, full rescans make 1,200 comparisons; the lookup stores 200 entries and receives 6 probes.

INTERACTIVE EXPERIMENT
One missing reply, two possible histories

Ada intends to buy two mugs. Five are available, so an accidental second purchase could succeed too. K14 identifies her original intent. Compare what actually happened inside the database with what the application knows.

Step through a committed purchase whose reply is lost. Try recovering with the same key, then with a new key. Finally change the hidden history to a rollback: the application receives the same missing answer.

RESULT
Starting state

Committed mugs available
5
Committed orders for this intent
0
Database reality

5 mugs available; no order for K14.

Application’s knowledge and action

Retains K14: Ada wants 2 mugs at €20 each.

This experiment starts with five mugs so an accidental second purchase can also succeed.

What this experiment models

If the original purchase committed, retaining K14 recovers one order while inventing K15 can create two. If the original purchase rolled back, either key can create one order. The application cannot choose a safe policy by assuming which hidden history occurred.
